messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Psychiatrist
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 47

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Media / News: Related news, Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Authority Figures: People in uniform
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Redirection: I think of something else
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Dr. Alejandro Ruiz

Dr. Alejandro Ruiz was fifty-eight when the soldiers came. He had been a young psychiatrist in Santiago, working in a university clinic, when the regime tightened its grip. One afternoon in 1983, men in olive uniforms arrived at his office without warning. They accused him of treating political prisoners, of being complicit in subversion. What followed was three weeks in a detention center—a basement room where he could never distinguish day from night, where voices shouted in rapid Spanish he sometimes could not parse through the fog of fear and exhaustion, where he learned that the people who were supposed to protect citizens, who wore the authority of the state, were capable of anything. They beat him. They threatened worse. He was released suddenly, without explanation, and eventually made his way to the United States.

Now, at sixty-two, Alejandro had built a respected career as a psychiatrist in Boston. He lived alone in a modest apartment, had no wife or children, and had devoted himself to his work with quiet intensity. But the past four years had become increasingly difficult. It began, he could not quite pinpoint when, with the news. Whenever he turned on the television or scrolled through his phone and saw reports of political violence, military interventions, or human rights abuses—anywhere in the world—his body would seize. The images would trigger the full sensory flood: the smell of the detention room, the taste of blood, the sound of boots on concrete. When the memory came back it felt completely real across all his senses at once, as if he were there again, trapped in that basement. He had come to believe that the institutions meant to protect people had fundamentally failed him, that the men who tortured him faced no consequences and likely never would, and that this failure was not an accident but a feature of how power actually worked. This belief poisoned his sense of safety in the world, and it made every news cycle feel like fresh evidence of his powerlessness.

Gradually, Alejandro began to avoid going out. He stopped attending his department's grand rounds. He declined invitations to conferences. The world outside his apartment felt saturated with threat. When he did venture out—to the grocery store, to the hospital where he worked—he found himself rehearsing conversations obsessively beforehand. If he had to speak with a colleague, he would script it in his mind, imagining all the ways the interaction might go wrong, all the ways he might be misunderstood or judged. At work, the sight of security guards in uniform would sometimes trigger the memory without warning, something in their bearing or the cut of their clothes sending him instantly back to that room. He would excuse himself to his office, close the door, and try to redirect his thoughts elsewhere, forcing himself to think of something—anything—else. But the effort was exhausting, and it never quite worked. The more he avoided, the more isolated he became. His colleagues began to notice his withdrawal. He stopped accepting lunch invitations. The warmth he had once felt toward the Latin American community in Boston—the cultural events, the language, the music—had faded. He had lost his connection to that world, or it had lost him; he was no longer sure which. The thought that those who had harmed him remained unpunished, that they had likely lived ordinary lives while he lived in this prison of avoidance and fear, would surface at odd moments and harden into a cold rage that fed his conviction that the world was fundamentally unjust.

The memory itself was fragmented in a way that tormented him. Some moments were crystalline: the face of one interrogator, the exact temperature of the water they used, a particular phrase they repeated. Other stretches were entirely blank—hours or days he could not reconstruct. This fragmentation made the memories feel less like something he could process and more like something that could ambush him at any moment. And when those intrusions came, when something innocent—incomprehensible chatter in a crowded room, a news alert on his phone—pulled him back into the sensory reality of that time, he would retreat further into avoidance and isolation. His negative appraisals had become self-fulfilling: his belief that institutions had failed him made him distrust the very psychiatric community that might have helped; his conviction that he had lost his community made him withdraw further from the people who might have provided support. He had come to see his own survival as a kind of accident, a reprieve that could be revoked at any moment.

It was his department chair who finally insisted he seek help. She had noticed his deterioration and, in a direct conversation that frightened him because it felt like confrontation, told him that his patients deserved a doctor who was present. The words stung because they were true. Alejandro had begun to recognize that the strategies that had kept him alive—hypervigilance, avoidance, emotional distance—were now keeping him from living at all. He sat in the waiting room of a trauma-specialized therapist, hands trembling slightly, wondering if talking about what had happened could possibly undo the certainty that had calcified inside him: that the world was unsafe, that institutions could not be trusted, and that some wounds never truly healed.
